title: THE FACE YOU CALLED THE ENEMY
paragraphs: THE FACE YOU CALLED THE ENEMY
What “Our Struggle Is Not Against Flesh and Blood” Changes About How You See the Person Who Hurt You
What if one of Satan’s most effective victories is not simply getting people to hurt each other…
…but convincing Christians that the person who hurt them is the enemy?
Read that again.
Because somewhere in your life, there may be a face you have attached to the word enemy.
The person who betrayed you.
The spouse who broke your trust.
The relative who keeps reopening wounds you thought had healed.
The church member who embarrassed you.
The pastor who disappointed you.
The friend who disappeared when you needed them.
The coworker who seems determined to make your life miserable.
The person whose political opinions make your blood boil.
The stranger online whose comment made something dark rise inside you.
You see their face.
You remember what they said.
You replay what they did.
And something inside you whispers:
That person is my enemy.
Then Paul walks into that battlefield with one sentence that changes the entire way a Christian is supposed to see human conflict:
“For we wrestle not against flesh and blood…”
Ephesians 6:12.
The Greek is even more arresting:
ὅτι οὐκ ἔστιν ἡμῖν ἡ πάλη πρὸς αἷμα καὶ σάρκα
Hoti ouk estin hēmin hē palē pros haima kai sarka.
The heart of the statement is unmistakable.
Our struggle—ἡ πάλη, hē palē—is not ultimately against αἷμα καὶ σάρκα, haima kai sarka: “blood and flesh,” the ordinary biblical way of referring to human beings in their mortal humanity.
Paul does not say there is no struggle.
That matters.
Christianity is not pretending everything is peaceful when it is not.
Paul uses the language of struggle, conflict, wrestling.
There really is a battle.
There really are wounds.
There really is evil.
There really are lies worth confronting.
There really are people who manipulate, deceive, betray, exploit, abuse, persecute, slander, and destroy.
But Paul reaches into our instinctive interpretation of conflict and says:
You are looking at the battlefield incorrectly.
Because the person standing in front of you is not the deepest enemy behind the war.
Paul continues:
“…but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places.”
This is not permission to become superstitious.
It is not permission to blame a demon every time somebody disagrees with you.
It is not permission to stop thinking carefully about psychology, trauma, consequences, justice, responsibility, or human choices.
And it certainly does not mean people are innocent of everything they do.
Scripture repeatedly holds human beings responsible for sin.
Judas betrayed Jesus.
Herod acted wickedly.
Pilate made decisions.
Religious leaders conspired.
People lied.
People murdered.
People persecuted.
Human responsibility does not disappear simply because spiritual evil exists.
But Ephesians 6 exposes something deeper.
Behind the visible conflicts of this fallen world stands an invisible kingdom of darkness that delights whenever hatred multiplies.
That means Satan does not necessarily need you to abandon Christianity publicly.
Sometimes he only needs you to hate someone privately.
He does not always need to make you deny Jesus.
Sometimes he only needs to make you despise someone Jesus told you to love.
And that is where this becomes painfully personal.
Because it is easy to read Ephesians 6:12 while imagining demons somewhere in the distance.
It is harder to read it while remembering the person you cannot forgive.
The person whose name changes your mood.
The person whose failure secretly makes you happy.
The person you hope gets exposed.
The person you have mentally sentenced a thousand times.
The person you have reduced to the worst thing they ever did.
Suddenly Paul’s words become uncomfortable.
Because perhaps the battle is not only happening around you.
Perhaps part of the battlefield is happening inside you.
You were wounded.
Then anger came.
Anger became resentment.
Resentment became rehearsed conversations.
Rehearsed conversations became assumptions.
Assumptions became contempt.
And eventually you stopped seeing a human being.
You saw an enemy.
That is exactly where the Gospel interrupts us.
Because Jesus Christ did something almost impossible for the human heart to understand.
He loved His enemies.
Not theoretically.
While nails were being driven through Him.
While people mocked Him.
While soldiers gambled for His clothing.
While religious leaders celebrated His suffering.
While the crowd watched.
Jesus prayed:
“Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.”
Luke 23:34.
That does not make crucifixion less evil.
It reveals how astonishing Christ is.
Jesus never confused forgiveness with pretending evil was good.
He called sin what it was.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He exposed corruption.
He warned of judgment.
He overturned tables.
He rebuked religious leaders.
And still…
He loved sinners enough to die for them.
This is where Christianity becomes more than inspirational language.
Because Jesus does not merely ask you to admire His mercy.
He commands His disciples to imitate it.
“Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you…”
Matthew 5:44.
That command feels beautiful until your enemy has a name.
Then Christianity becomes costly.
Love your enemies.
That one too, Lord?
Pray for those who persecute you.
After what they did?
Forgive.
But they never apologized.
Bless.
But they tried to destroy me.
And perhaps your heart answers:
Jesus, You don't understand.
Except He does.
He understands betrayal.
Judas kissed Him.
He understands abandonment.
His disciples ran.
He understands false accusations.
Witnesses lied.
He understands humiliation.
Soldiers mocked Him.
He understands physical suffering.
They scourged Him.
He understands public shame.
They stripped Him.
He understands injustice.
An innocent Man was condemned.
He understands rejection.
His own people cried for His crucifixion.
And from the cross, Jesus showed us something terrifyingly beautiful:
You can recognize evil without becoming consumed by hatred for the person committing it.
That is spiritual warfare.
Sometimes spiritual warfare looks less like shouting at darkness and more like refusing to let darkness reproduce itself inside you.
Read that slowly.
Sometimes the enemy hurts you through someone else…
and then tries to recruit you through the wound.
Someone sins against you.
Now bitterness wants you.
Someone humiliates you.
Now vengeance wants you.
Someone lies about you.
Now hatred wants you.
Someone abandons you.
Now hardness wants you.
The first wound may have been inflicted by another person.
But the next battle happens inside your heart.
And this is why Paul does not merely tell Christians who the enemy is.
He tells them what to wear.
Truth.
Righteousness.
The readiness of the Gospel of peace.
Faith.
Salvation.
The Word of God.
Prayer.
Notice what is missing.
Hatred.
There is no belt of hatred.
No breastplate of revenge.
No helmet of superiority.
No shield of contempt.
No sword of humiliation.
No armor piece called “winning the argument.”
The armor of God looks remarkably unlike the weapons we instinctively reach for.
Because the kingdom of Jesus does not defeat darkness by becoming darker.
It overcomes evil with good.
That is exactly what Romans 12:21 says:
“Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.”
There are two ways evil can defeat you.
It can destroy you from outside.
Or it can convince you to become like it from inside.
The second victory may be far more dangerous.
Because you can survive somebody’s cruelty and still allow bitterness to reshape your soul.
You can leave the abusive relationship and carry the abuser inside your thoughts for twenty years.
You can block the number while still replaying the conversation every night.
You can move churches while resentment moves with you.
You can win the court case and lose your peace.
You can prove that you were right and slowly become someone you no longer recognize.
Forgiveness does not mean pretending none of it happened.
And this must be said carefully.
If someone is abusing you, Ephesians 6:12 does not command you to remain available for abuse.
If someone is dangerous, loving them does not require giving them unrestricted access to you.
If a crime has been committed, forgiveness does not mean preventing legitimate authorities from pursuing justice.
Romans 13 recognizes the proper role of governing authority.
Jesus Himself sometimes withdrew from people who intended Him harm.
Paul escaped dangerous situations.
Biblical forgiveness and biblical wisdom are not enemies.
You can forgive and establish boundaries.
You can love someone and refuse to enable them.
You can pray for someone and still testify truthfully about what they did.
You can desire somebody’s salvation while also recognizing that reconciliation requires more than pretending trust was never shattered.
Forgiveness releases personal vengeance into God's hands.
Reconciliation ordinarily requires truth, repentance, and restored trust.
And trust may take time.
Sometimes wisdom means distance.
But distance does not require hatred.
That distinction could set someone free tonight.
Because perhaps you thought forgiveness meant saying:
It didn't matter.
No.
The cross proves sin matters enormously.
Forgiveness says:
It mattered so much that I cannot heal it by pretending it was nothing. But I refuse to become the permanent prisoner of what you did to me. I surrender vengeance to God.
That is different.
And maybe this article found you while you are carrying somebody.
Not physically.
Inside you.
Their voice.
Their betrayal.
Their accusation.
Their rejection.
Their affair.
Their abandonment.
Their cruelty.
Their hypocrisy.
Their failure.
Their name has been living rent-free in your nervous system.
You wake up and remember.
You lie down and replay it.
You imagine conversations that never happen.
You imagine apologies they may never give.
You imagine finally saying the sentence that will make them understand how badly they hurt you.
And underneath everything is a quiet question:
How could they do this to me?
But perhaps Jesus is asking another question tonight.
What is this doing to you?
Because the enemy would gladly use another person's sin to build a prison inside your soul.
And every time you rehearse hatred, another brick goes up.
Every fantasy of revenge adds another.
Every moment of contempt adds another.
Until eventually the person who wounded you may have moved on…
but you are still living inside the cell.
Jesus came to open prison doors.
Not merely the obvious ones.
The invisible ones too.
This is why the Gospel changes how Christians see people.
Every human being you meet bears the dignity of being made in the image of God.
Every human being is fallen.
Every human being desperately needs grace.
And every human being—including the one writing this and the one reading it—is capable of becoming the villain in someone else's story.
That should humble us.
Because before the Gospel tells you to forgive your enemies, it tells you something even more devastating:
You were once God's enemy.
Romans 5 says:
“For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son…”
When we were enemies.
Not when we had cleaned ourselves up.
Not when we had finally become lovable.
Not when we had earned another chance.
Enemies.
And Christ died for us.
That changes everything.
Christian forgiveness does not begin with how deserving the other person is.
It begins with remembering how undeserving we were.
The cross destroys our ability to stand beneath Jesus receiving mercy while simultaneously standing over everyone else demanding payment.
We owed a debt we could never repay.
Jesus paid it.
We stood guilty.
Jesus showed mercy.
We wandered.
Jesus pursued.
We rebelled.
Jesus loved.
We sinned.
Jesus bled.
And now the forgiven become forgivers.
Not because evil suddenly becomes acceptable.
Because grace has become unforgettable.
This is the scandal of grace.
The murderer can repent.
The adulterer can repent.
The addict can repent.
The liar can repent.
The hypocrite can repent.
The religious fraud can repent.
The prodigal can come home.
The bitter Christian can repent too.
Nobody is beyond the reach of Christ while there is breath and opportunity to turn to Him.
That does not erase earthly consequences.
Grace is not the cancellation of truth.
Grace is God meeting guilty people in truth and offering them what they could never purchase for themselves.
Forgiveness.
Cleansing.
A new heart.
A new identity.
A new life.
This is why you cannot look at people exactly the same after understanding Ephesians 6:12.
The atheist arguing with you online is not your ultimate enemy.
The unbelieving relative mocking your faith is not your ultimate enemy.
The Christian who disappointed you is not your ultimate enemy.
The person trapped in sexual sin is not your ultimate enemy.
The addict is not your ultimate enemy.
The political opponent is not your ultimate enemy.
The angry teenager is not your ultimate enemy.
The confused skeptic is not your ultimate enemy.
The prodigal child is not your ultimate enemy.
They may oppose you.
They may sin against you.
They may believe destructive things.
They may need correction.
They may require boundaries.
They may even require legal accountability.
But they are still people for whom Christ's Gospel must be proclaimed.
And once you understand that, evangelism changes.
You stop trying merely to win arguments.
You start longing to win people.
You stop treating unbelievers as interruptions to Christian culture.
You begin seeing them as souls.
You stop celebrating when opponents collapse.
You start wondering whether brokenness might become the doorway through which they finally cry out to Jesus.
Imagine if the Church remembered this.
Imagine Christians who could confront lies without hating liars.
Expose darkness without becoming cruel.
Defend truth without losing tenderness.
Practice discernment without developing contempt.
Stand against evil without forgetting the humanity of those trapped inside it.
Imagine believers who actually believed that conversion is possible.
Because Saul once breathed threats against Christians.
Then Jesus met him.
And the persecutor became Paul.
Think about that.
If the early Christians had only seen Saul according to what he had done, they would have seen a monster.
Jesus saw what grace could make him.
That does not mean Christians should naively place themselves in danger.
Acts itself records the understandable fear believers initially had toward Saul.
But grace wrote another chapter.
That is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior:
Maybe that is why you should hesitate before declaring that somebody will “never change.”
You do not know what Jesus may do with the next chapter.
And perhaps the person most urgently needing another chapter is not the person who hurt you.
Perhaps it is you.
Maybe bitterness has exhausted you.
Maybe hatred has become strangely comforting because it feels safer than grief.
Maybe anger has protected you from admitting how deeply you were wounded.
Maybe you have told everybody you are “over it,” but one mention of their name proves otherwise.
You do not have to pretend tonight.
Jesus already knows.
Bring Him the ugly prayer.
Lord, I don't want to forgive them.
Bring Him the honest prayer.
Lord, part of me still wants them to hurt.
Bring Him the exhausted prayer.
Lord, I cannot carry this anymore.
Bring Him the frightened prayer.
Lord, if I release this anger, I don't know what will be left.
You do not impress Christ by hiding wounds from the One who bears scars.
Bring Him everything.
Then remember:
Forgiveness is not pretending justice does not matter.
It is refusing to make yourself God.
“Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.”
Romans 12:19.
You can put the gavel down.
God has not surrendered His throne.
He sees what happened.
He knows what was said.
He knows what was stolen.
He knows what was hidden.
He knows what nobody believed.
He knows what you cannot prove.
And because He is Judge, you do not have to become one in your heart every morning.
Release them to Him.
Again tomorrow if necessary.
And again the day after that.
Sometimes forgiveness is a decisive act followed by a long healing process.
But every surrender declares something to hell:
You will not turn their sin into mine.
That is warfare.
When hatred says, “Destroy them,” and the Spirit leads you to pray for them…
warfare.
When bitterness says, “Replay it,” and you surrender the memory to Christ…
warfare.
When pride says, “You would never do what they did,” and the cross reminds you that you live by mercy too…
warfare.
When Satan says, “That person is beyond redemption,” and you remember Saul of Tarsus…
warfare.
When shame says, “You are beyond redemption,” and you remember the blood of Jesus…
warfare.
Because Ephesians 6 was never given so Christians could become fascinated with darkness.
It was given so Christians could stand in Christ.
And perhaps this is where the story turns.
You thought this article was about the person who hurt you.
Maybe Jesus has been talking about your heart the whole time.
Not condemning you.
Calling you out of captivity.
You cannot change what they did.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
You cannot force repentance.
You cannot manufacture reconciliation.
You cannot make someone understand your pain.
But through Christ, yesterday does not have to own tomorrow.
That is what Jesus does.
He walks into scandals and writes grace.
He walks into graves and writes resurrection.
He walks into shame and writes redemption.
He walks into bondage and writes freedom.
He walks into ruined people and begins making them new.
And He can walk into this wound too.
If something hidden was exposed while you read this, don't rush past it.
Somebody reading silently may desperately need evidence that healing is possible.
Then think of one person who needs this truth.
Not twenty.
One.
Maybe they have been consumed by family conflict.
Maybe betrayal is eating them alive.
Maybe politics has taught them to hate strangers.
Maybe church hurt has pushed them toward abandoning Jesus.
Maybe they are fighting a person when the deeper battle is for their own heart.
Send this article privately if their wound is too personal for a public tag.
Because forgiveness is rarely a lesson we need only once.
Tomorrow the memory may return.
When it does, come back and remember:
Flesh and blood are not the ultimate enemy.

If Gospel Warrior has helped you encounter Scripture, conviction, encouragement, healing, repentance, and the truth of Jesus Christ, you can also help this ministry keep putting Gospel-centered resources in front of people who need them.
Supporting Gospel ministry is not a substitute for worship, obedience, generosity to your local church, caring for your family, or serving people around you.
Your support helps us keep pointing wounded people toward Jesus.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the believer who is struggling.
Invite the lukewarm Christian who needs awakening.
Invite the seeker with questions.
Invite even the unbeliever who thinks Jesus could never want someone like them.
Live it.
Because somewhere soon, somebody is going to offend you.
Somebody will misunderstand you.
Somebody may wound you.
And when their face appears in your mind, remember Paul's words:
“Our struggle is not against flesh and blood.”
See the sin clearly.
Tell the truth.
Set boundaries when necessary.
Seek justice where appropriate.
Protect the vulnerable.
Refuse manipulation.
Do not call darkness light.
But never surrender your heart to hatred.
Look at people through the shadow of a cross where the Son of God died for His enemies.
And remember that once…
you needed that mercy too.
Maybe the greatest evidence that Christ has won the battle is not that your enemy finally falls.
Maybe it is that after everything they did to you, Jesus refused to let hatred have the final word in you.
